summary: Describes DomainKeys, a way to sign email per domain using public-key cryptography, with the keys published in the DNS. The aim is to prove where a message came from and that it was not altered. It is historic, replaced by DKIM in RFC 4871.

eli5.summary: A company puts a seal on every letter and publishes a picture of the seal where anyone can look it up. Readers compare the two. This old idea was replaced by a newer one.

questions: how to sign email with domainkeys
subtitle: Sign email with public keys published in the DNS to prove it came from a domain.

tldr.problem: Email is easy to forge because there is no standard way to prove who actually sent a message. Spammers and phishers exploit this to impersonate legitimate senders.
tldr.mechanism: DomainKeys lets a domain owner publish public keys in the DNS under a special namespace, sign outgoing email with the corresponding private keys, and add the signature to the email header. Recipients can fetch the public key and verify that the email really came from the domain.
tldr.outcome: Receiving systems can now authenticate email at the domain level and apply policy based on whether a signature is valid or missing. DomainKeys was superseded by DKIM (RFC 4871), which improved the design.

today: RFC 4870 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 4871, which defines DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail). DKIM is based on DomainKeys but includes improvements for real-world email handling. DKIM is now the standard email authentication mechanism deployed by major email systems worldwide.

sections.title: The Problem: Unauthenticated Email
sections.content:
Internet email was designed in an era of mostly trusted users on directly connected networks. There was no built-in way to verify who actually sent a message or prove that the message was not altered in transit. Today, this has become a serious vulnerability: spammers and phishers routinely forge the From: header to make their messages appear to come from legitimate domains. The recipient has no way to know whether the message is genuine.

DomainKeys is a domain-level authentication framework designed to solve this problem. It uses public key cryptography and the DNS to let domain owners prove that email claiming to come from their domain actually came from an authorized sender.
sections.eli5: Email can be faked because there is no signature to prove where it came from. DomainKeys adds a signature that email readers can check against the real sender's domain.

sections.title: How DomainKeys Works
sections.content:
DomainKeys operates by having a domain owner generate a pair of cryptographic keys (one private, one public). The domain publishes the public key in the DNS under a special namespace reserved for DomainKeys: _domainkey. When the domain sends email, the outbound mail system uses the private key to digitally sign the message using RSA and SHA-1. The signature is added to the email as a DomainKey-Signature: header.

When a receiving system gets an email claiming to come from a domain, it can extract the signature from the header, fetch the published public key from the DNS, and verify that the signature is valid. If the signature is valid, the receiving system knows the email came from someone authorized by the domain. If the signature is invalid or missing, the receiving system can look up the domain's policy in the DNS to decide how to handle it.
sections.eli5: The sending domain has two keys: a secret one it keeps private, and a public one it announces. The secret key signs each message, and the public key lets readers check that the signature is real.

sections.title: Keys and Signatures
sections.content:
DomainKeys uses selectors to support multiple public keys per domain. A selector is an arbitrary name that identifies a particular key or key pair. This allows a domain to maintain multiple concurrent keys (for example, one per geographic region or per server) and rotate them by publishing a new selector while the old one is still valid. The DNS lookup path combines the selector, the domain, and the reserved _domainkey namespace: for example, brisbane._domainkey.example.com might hold the public key for the Brisbane server.

Public keys are stored in DNS TXT records as Base64-encoded values in a tag-value format. The default signing algorithm is RSA with a SHA-1 digest, and verifiers must support key sizes of 512, 768, 1024, 1536 and 2048 bits. The signature header itself is also stored as tag-value pairs and includes the algorithm used, the selector, the signing domain, the canonicalization algorithm, and the Base64-encoded signature data.
sections.eli5: Selectors are like numbered keys: a domain can have key 2005, key 2006, and so on, so it can change keys without breaking anything.

sections.title: Handling Email Modifications
sections.content:
Email messages often change as they travel through the Internet: mail servers might reformat headers, adjust line breaks, or modify whitespace. These changes can invalidate a signature. To solve this, DomainKeys defines two canonicalization algorithms that prepare the email for signing and verification in a predictable way that tolerates common, harmless modifications.

The simple algorithm includes all headers and the body as-is, removing only trailing empty lines and normalizing line endings. The nofws (No Folding Whitespace) algorithm is more forgiving: it removes unnecessary whitespace from all lines and unwraps header continuation lines. A signer chooses which algorithm to use when creating the signature, and verifiers must support both. This allows senders to choose how much in-transit modification they are willing to tolerate.
sections.eli5: Email gets shuffled around as it travels. DomainKeys has two ways of preparing the message so a shuffle does not break the signature: a strict way and a forgiving way.

sections.title: Verification and Policy
sections.content:
When a receiving system verifies an email, it extracts the signature information from the DomainKey-Signature: header, uses the selector and domain from the header to fetch the public key from the DNS, and checks whether the signature is valid using the canonicalization algorithm specified in the header. If verification succeeds, the system knows the email was authorized by that domain. If it fails or there is no signature, the receiving system can look up the domain's _domainkey policy record to learn the domain's preferences.

Domain policy records are also stored in DNS as tag-value pairs. A domain can indicate whether it signs all outbound email (which might make recipients reject unsigned messages), whether it is in testing mode (to avoid penalties during rollout), and where to send verification failure reports. This allows domain owners to guide recipient systems on how to handle authentication results.
sections.eli5: If the signature checks out, the email is real. If it does not, the receiving system can ask the domain's DNS record what to do about it.

sections.title: Historical Status and Succession
sections.content:
DomainKeys was published in May 2007 as a Proposed Standard and proved successful in practice. However, it was marked Historic shortly after when it was superseded by RFC 4871, which defines DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail). DKIM is based on the DomainKeys design but makes several improvements, including better handling of mailing lists, stronger canonicalization algorithms, and clearer specifications.

Although DomainKeys itself is no longer the recommended standard, the concepts and mechanisms it introduced became the foundation for DKIM, which is now the dominant email authentication standard deployed by major email providers worldwide.
sections.eli5: DomainKeys was later replaced by a better version called DKIM that works even better for things like mailing lists.
